slides.title: Origins
slides.say:
STORY (3 January 2009): The first Bitcoin block ever mined carries a piece of that morning's newspaper: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks'. It proves the block could not have been made earlier than that headline, and at the same time records why the system was built - in the middle of a banking crisis, by someone who wanted money that needs no bailout and no bank.
SOURCE: Bitcoin genesis block coinbase text, block 0, 2009-01-03; The Times front page of 3 January 2009; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin (genesis block).
slides.takeaway: Three stories that explain why Bitcoin looks the way it does

slides.title: The first person ever paid in bitcoin
slides.say:
STORY (January 2009): Nine days after the genesis block, Satoshi Nakamoto sent 10 bitcoin to Hal Finney, a veteran cryptographer who had answered the whitepaper with curiosity instead of dismissal and famously tweeted 'Running bitcoin'. Finney had worked on PGP and had built the first reusable proof-of-work system years before Bitcoin existed - the first payment went to someone who had spent a career preparing for it.
SOURCE: Bitcoin block 170, 2009-01-12, the first bitcoin transaction (Satoshi Nakamoto to Hal Finney, 10 BTC); Hal Finney, 'Running bitcoin', twitter.com/halfin, 2009-01-10.
slides.takeaway: Peer to peer meant person to person from day one

slides.title: Forty years of failed digital money
slides.say:
STORY (1982 - 2008): Bitcoin was not a first attempt. David Chaum designed blind-signature ecash in the 1980s and his company DigiCash went bankrupt; Adam Back built Hashcash's proof-of-work in 1997 to price email spam; Wei Dai sketched b-money and Nick Szabo bit gold in 1998, both unbuilt for want of a way to agree without a leader. Satoshi's 2008 whitepaper cites them and adds the missing piece - proof-of-work as the voting weight of an open network - turning four decades of near-misses into a running system.
SOURCE: S. Nakamoto, 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' (2008), references; A. Back, Hashcash (1997); W. Dai, b-money (1998); N. Szabo, bit gold; D. Chaum, 'Blind signatures for untraceable payments' (1982).
slides.takeaway: The pieces were old; the combination was new

slides.title: Money
slides.say:
SAY: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Money.
slides.takeaway: What the currency is, who issues it, and on what schedule

slides.title: The island where money never moved
slides.say:
STORY (Yap, documented 1903): On the island of Yap, wealth was held in rai - limestone discs up to four metres wide, far too heavy to move. When a stone changed owners, the stone stayed where it lay; what changed was the community's shared memory of who owned it. One famous stone sank to the sea floor in transit, and the islanders kept trading it anyway, because everyone agreed it existed and whose it was.
SOURCE: W. H. Furness III, The Island of Stone Money (1910); Milton Friedman, 'The Island of Stone Money', Hoover Institution Working Paper E-91-3 (1991).

read.label: Furness: The Island of Stone Money (book)

slides.takeaway: Money is a ledger; Bitcoin makes it digital

slides.title: Five thousand years to digital cash
slides.say:
STORY (c. 3000 BCE - 2009): Money keeps changing form: grain-ledger entries in Mesopotamia, the first struck coins in Lydia around 600 BCE, paper notes in Song-dynasty China, goldsmiths' receipts becoming bank money, and in 1971 the dollar's last tie to gold cut, leaving pure fiat. Cards and online banking then made most money digital - but always as entries in some institution's private ledger. Cryptocurrency is the next step on the same road: money that is only a ledger, but a public one no single institution keeps.
SOURCE: Standard monetary history: Lydian electrum coinage (c. 7th-6th century BCE); Song-dynasty jiaozi paper money; the 1971 Nixon gold-convertibility suspension; Mastering Bitcoin 3e, ch. 1, on bitcoin as digital money.
slides.takeaway: Each era changed the ledger-keeper; Bitcoin removed the position

slides.title: Physical cash: superb in person, stuck there
slides.say:
SAY: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Which of these failures did cards fix - and at what new price?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Money.
slides.takeaway: Cash is a bearer instrument: perfect in person, useless on a network

slides.title: The internet got payments - and new gatekeepers
slides.say:
STORY (1998 - 2002): The web could sell before it could pay: cards were unsafe to type and banks had no internet rails. Confinity, founded 1998 by Max Levchin and Peter Thiel, and X.com, founded 1999 by Elon Musk, raced to fix it, merged in 2000, and became PayPal - sold to eBay for 1.5 billion dollars in 2002. The same boom's pure digital currencies, Beenz and Flooz, died in the 2001 crash, taking their customers' balances with them. Online payment was solved, but only as accounts on one company's private ledger - the internet still had no cash.
SOURCE: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PayPal (Confinity 1998, X.com 1999, merger 2000, eBay acquisition 2002); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flooz.com and /wiki/Beenz.com (both closed 2001 in the dot-com crash).
IMAGE: the PayPal wordmark (public domain, via Wikimedia Commons) - the one survivor of the slide's timeline.
slides.takeaway: Payments went online in 1998-2002; cash never did

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.say:
STORY (2007 - 2022): Money fails people in documented ways. Kenya, 2007: most adults had no bank, so Safaricom's M-Pesa turned phone credit into the country's money rail. Cyprus, March 2013: banks closed for days and a levy took part of large deposits overnight. Greece, summer 2015: capital controls capped ATM withdrawals at 60 euros a day. Venezuela, 2018: hyperinflation passed one million percent and wages evaporated between morning and evening. Ukraine, February 2022: with war at the capital, the government itself posted donation addresses and raised tens of millions of dollars in crypto within days, run by Deputy Minister Alex Bornyakov, when ordinary rails were too slow.
SOURCE: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Pesa (Safaricom, 2007); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012-2013_Cypriot_financial_crisis (deposit levy, March 2013); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_government-debt_crisis (2015 capital controls, 60-euro limit); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Venezuela (over 1,000,000% in 2018); CNBC 2022-03-02 and Fortune 2022-03-26 on Ukraine's official crypto donations (Alex Bornyakov, 35 million dollars within the first week).
slides.takeaway: Crisis or war, banked or not - the need is documented, not theoretical

slides.title: Why digital money had to wait
slides.say:
SAY: The double-spend is the act of spending the same unit of digital money more than once. The chapter lists it as the second of three basic questions for anyone accepting digital money: can I trust that the digital money can only be spent once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Why does the same problem not exist for paper cash?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - DoubleSpend.
slides.takeaway: Perfect copies made digital cash impossible without a referee

slides.title: One bitcoin divides into 100 million satoshis
slides.say:
SAY: The Unit section answers the first question that any money raises, namely what the money is called and in what pieces it is counted. It contains the name of the currency, with its distinction between the unit and the system, and the smallest subdivision that can be recorded, the satoshi.
ASK: How many satoshis buy a coffee at today's price?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Unit.
slides.takeaway: Money here is counting, and the units are exact

slides.title: 21 million, by rule - not by promise
slides.say:
SAY: The Supply section is about how much bitcoin exists and how the amount grows. The chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, limiting the total to a fixed number just below 21 million, so that the number in circulation follows a predictable curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Why does the sum stop just short of 21 million?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Supply, Issuance.
DATES: genesis 2009-01-03; halvings 2012-11-28 (block 210,000), 2016-07-09 (420,000), 2020-05-11 (630,000), 2024-04-20 (840,000) - the blocks' own timestamps; later dates are projections at the 10-minute target. Table: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply
slides.takeaway: Scarcity is enforced by arithmetic every node checks

slides.title: Price is discovered, not declared
slides.say:
SAY: The Price section addresses a question that every newcomer asks, namely who sets the price of bitcoin. The chapter's short answer is that the price is set by markets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Price.
slides.takeaway: No one sets the price; everyone does

slides.title: Two pizzas for ten thousand bitcoin
slides.say:
STORY (22 May 2010): For Bitcoin's first year and a half, nobody knew what a bitcoin was worth, because nobody had ever bought anything with one. Then Laszlo Hanyecz, a Florida programmer, offered 10,000 BTC on a forum to anyone who would bring him two pizzas - and someone did. That order, the first known commercial purchase paid in bitcoin, is why 22 May is still celebrated as Bitcoin Pizza Day: it is the day a floating price began to exist.
SOURCE: Guinness World Records, 'First commercial Bitcoin transaction' (Laszlo Hanyecz, 2010-05-22, 10,000 BTC for two pizzas); bitcointalk.org thread 'Pizza for bitcoins?', May 2010.
slides.takeaway: Price is discovered the first time someone pays

slides.title: The pizza, repriced every few years
slides.say:
SAY: Every point is a documented milestone - dollar parity in 2011, the first thousand in 2013, the 2017 and 2021 peaks - and the last one was fetched live from mempool.space and CoinGecko while this deck was built, agreeing within 0.1 percent.

slides.title: Wallets and first use
slides.say:
SAY: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin. The chapter calls the Bitcoin wallet the most common user interface to the Bitcoin system, just as a web browser is the most common user interface for the protocol of the web, and the glossary of the book describes it as software that holds your Bitcoin addresses and secret keys and lets you send, receive and store your bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Your key is your deed - and you may never show it
slides.say:
SAY: Key control is the question of who holds the private keys that unlock a wallet's funds. The chapter calls this a very important additional consideration and says that access to bitcoins is controlled by private keys, which are like very long PINs.
ASK: Your house has a registry if the key is lost - what does bitcoin have?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - KeyControl.
slides.takeaway: Prove you hold the key; never reveal it

slides.title: Who holds the keys, holds the coins
slides.say:
SAY: Key control is the question of who holds the private keys that unlock a wallet's funds. The chapter calls this a very important additional consideration and says that access to bitcoins is controlled by private keys, which are like very long PINs.
ASK: Which side was the exchange that lost its customers' coins on?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - KeyControl, WalletPlatform, Backup.
slides.takeaway: Custody is the first security decision you make

slides.title: Mt. Gox: the exchange that lost everyone's coins
slides.say:
STORY (February 2014): Mt. Gox of Tokyo, led by Mark Karpeles, was once the world's largest bitcoin exchange, handling the large majority of all trades. In February 2014 it halted withdrawals, filed for bankruptcy and admitted that around 850,000 bitcoins held on customers' behalf were gone - the customers had balances on a website, but the keys, and therefore the coins, had been in someone else's hands all along. Creditors were still being repaid more than a decade later.
SOURCE: Mt. Gox bankruptcy filing, Tokyo District Court, 2014-02-28, reporting approximately 850,000 BTC missing (about 750,000 of them customers'); widely reported, e.g. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Gox.
slides.takeaway: Whoever holds the keys holds the coins - exchanges included

slides.title: From a phrase to a key, slowly on purpose
slides.say:
SAY: The Backup section is about getting a wallet back after something goes wrong. It begins with the chapter's account of Alice's first start-up, when her noncustodial wallet produces a recovery code that can be used to restore it, and it goes on to the additional data that a recovery code does not contain, and to the payments that some technologies keep outside the public blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Backup, KeyControl.
slides.takeaway: Slowness here is a feature priced against attackers

slides.title: Foundations
slides.say:
SAY: The Foundations branch collects the general technical ideas that the rest of the chapter takes for granted. Chapter 1 of the textbook introduces Bitcoin through a story about Alice and Joe, and in doing so it uses words such as digital signature, private key, blockchain, node, protocol and QR code as if every reader already knew them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Foundations.
slides.takeaway: The two old problems Bitcoin finally joined up

slides.title: From keys to the chain
slides.say:
SAY: The Chain section explains the data structure at the centre of Bitcoin and the computers that maintain it. The block is a group of transactions that the network accepts together, the blockchain is the list of blocks linked one to the next, the timestamp is the mark of time that orders them, and the node is a computer that takes part in the network.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Chain, Cryptography.
slides.takeaway: This pipeline is the course syllabus in one row

slides.title: The toolbox under the hood
slides.say:
SAY: The Computing section explains the ordinary technology on which Bitcoin software runs and by which people reach it. It covers the internet and the rules that computers follow on it, the way programs talk to each other through interfaces, the way data is named and stored, the operating systems and browsers in which wallets live, and the units in which computers count.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Computing, Threats.
slides.takeaway: Every term here gets its own page section

slides.title: What kind of thing is Bitcoin?
slides.say:
SAY: The Nature branch answers a question that precedes all the others: what kind of thing is Bitcoin? Chapter 1 gives two complementary answers.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Nature, Characteristic, Architecture.
slides.takeaway: Each adjective is engineered, not advertised

slides.title: Beyond the base layer
slides.say:
SAY: The Transfer section explains what happens when Joe sends bitcoin to Alice. It follows the payment from the moment he presses Send to the moment it is confirmed in a block, and it introduces the objects and ideas involved: the transaction, its inputs and outputs, the fee, the confirmation, the irreversibility, and the newer payments that never reach the public chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Transfer, SemanticBridge.
slides.takeaway: The chain settles; the edges scale
